source_refs.note: Topic 3.2, printed pages 49-51: history of cell theory, its three points, its validation and its exceptions. Figure 3.1 (Hooke's microscope) is a picture and is covered in the text.

blocks.text: At the beginning of the 17th century, many scientists began to use microscopes to study very small objects. In 1665 the English scientist Robert Hooke examined a thin slice of cork of the oak tree under a microscope. He observed that the cork was made of "many little boxes". Hooke also examined pieces of the stem and root of the oak tree and found that these too were made of similar little boxes. He concluded that the parts of plants were made of compartments, and named these compartments "cellulae".

blocks.alt: Drawing of Robert Hooke's microscope: a long tilted tube on a pillar above a round base, with a piece of cork held on a pin below the objective end. Beside it, a circular view of a thin slice of cork showing many small, closed, box-like cells sharing their walls.

blocks.text: After these studies biologists began to organise information about cells. The observations of Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow were combined into a basic theory about cells, the cell theory. It has three essential points.

blocks.title: Cell theory
blocks.text: 1. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells. 2. Cells are the basic units of structure and function in an organism. 3. Cells come only from the division of pre-existing cells.
Cell theory can be validated through several observations and experiments.

items: By using light microscopes and electron microscopes, scientists visualise cell structures and find tangible evidence that cells are indeed the structural units of all living organisms.

Through techniques like live-cell imaging and genetic studies, scientists can track how cells replicate and give rise to new cells. These techniques validate the principle that all cells originate from pre-existing cells.
Techniques like DNA sequencing reveal that cells share common genetic material and metabolic pathways, reinforcing the notion that the cell is the fundamental unit of life.
Experiments such as cell culture studies and tissue engineering validate cell theory by demonstrating cellular growth, differentiation and reproduction.

blocks.text: While cell theory is widely accepted, there are notable exceptions.

items: Viruses challenge cell theory because they are not made of cells and cannot carry out life processes independently. They require a host cell to replicate and are considered by many scientists to be at the border of living and non-living. Similarly, prions and viroids show properties of living organisms but are not composed of cells; they are made only of DNA, RNA or proteins.

The eukaryotic organelles mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA and can replicate independently of the cell's nucleus. This suggests they may have originated from free-living prokaryotic cells.

Some organisms, such as certain fungi and algae, have structures where multiple nuclei coexist within a shared cytoplasmic mass. These blur the boundaries of individual cells as defined by traditional cell theory.
Muscle cells (myocytes) in vertebrates can fuse to form multinucleated fibres, challenging the concept of a single cell as the basic unit in complex tissues.
